#### [Exercise 1.7](#ex17q) {-}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item The distribution of hazelnut masses appears to be positively (right) skewed.
    \item The distribution of tree heights appears to be symmetrical, and may be approximately normal.
    \item The distribution of the number of patients appears to be negatively (left) skewed.
    \item The distribution of waiting times appears to be approximately uniform.
    \item The distribution of the number of successful passes appears to be bimodal but not symmetrical.
    \item The distribution of distances to the city centre appears to be bimodal and symmetrical.
\end{enumerate}

#### Chapter 3 Answers - Sampling Theory {-}

[]{#ex31a}

#### [Exercise 3.1](#ex31q) {-}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Sampling-frame issue:} The accessible group consists only of pupils entering the mathematics corridor at that time. Pupils elsewhere in the school, absent pupils and late pupils have no opportunity to be selected. The selected sample of pupils may therefore \textbf{not be representative} of the target population.\\[0.5em] \textbf{Sampling-method issue:} Selecting the first 20 pupils is \textbf{not random}. Early arrivals may differ from later arrivals, and groups arriving together may not be independent in their responses, so the sample may be \textbf{biased}.
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item All the people who use his local supermarket.
            \item All shoppers who use the self-checkout tills on that Sunday morning.
        \end{enumerate}
        \item The sampling frame excludes people who prefer to shop at other times, such as during the evening or midweek. It also only includes those using self-checkout tills, likely excluding those who have a large trolley of shopping. Both of these issues may introduce bias, and could lead to a sample unrepresentative of the target population.
        \item The sampling method is non-random and so may introduce bias to the sample, making it unrepresentative of the population and unreliable for statistical inference.
    \end{enumerate}
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item There may be so many flowers that it is too time-consuming and impractical to make a sampling frame made up of individual flowers.
        \item A better choice of sampling unit may be areas of the field, such as one-square-metre quadrats, forming a numbered grid from which quadrats may be randomly selected.
        \item A random number generator will help minimise a source of possible bias in the selection of quadrats to include in the sample, by ensuring it is random and not influenced by the botanist. It should help produce a sample that is may be more representative of the population of wildflowers.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

[]{#ex32a}

#### [Exercise 3.2](#ex32q) {-}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item
    \begin{multicols}{3}
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item One-stage cluster sampling.
        \item Stratified sampling.
        \item Systematic sampling.
        \item Simple random sampling.
        \item Quota sampling.
        \item Convenience sampling.
    \end{enumerate}
    \end{multicols}
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Each of the different types of room may have its own distinct characteristics in terms of ageing or the quality of maintenance. Stratified sampling will ensure that a proportionate number from each type of room will be included in the sample.
        \item 30 out of 360 cabins means 1 in every 12 cabins should be sampled, so the sample should contain: 2 Deluxe cabins; 6 Premium cabins and 22 Standard cabins. To sample the Deluxe cabins, a numbered list of those cabins should be obtained as a suitable sampling frame, and then a random number generator used to produce 2 different random numbers. Those cabins corresponding to the numbers selected should be included in the sample. This process should then be repeated for the Premium cabins and the Standard cabins, using a numbered sampling frame for each and randomly selecting the appropriate number of cabins of each type. The selected cabins are then combined to form the stratified sample.
    \end{enumerate}
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Convenience sampling.
        \item He only samples coral reefs close to his town, ignoring the fact that those near other towns or villages, or rural locations, may have a different level of health. This means the sample is unlikely to be representative of the population of coral reefs along the West Coast of Scotland. (Alternatively, the non-random selection method may be discussed.)
    \end{enumerate}
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Using cluster sampling means less physical travelling to a larger number of petrol stations, which would cost more and take more time.
        \item To sample approximately 40 pumps, 5 petrol stations are needed if one-stage cluster sampling is used, since each station typically has 8 pumps. A sampling frame of all the petrol stations numbered from 1 to 126 should be drawn up. A random number generator can then be used to select 5 numbers, and the petrol stations corresponding to those numbers should be included in the sample. From each of those petrol stations, all of the pumps should be sampled.
    \end{enumerate}
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Systematic sampling.
        \item She didn't use a random starting point, so it is not a true random sampling process.
    \end{enumerate}
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Quota sampling.
        \item This is a non-random sampling method which is liable to produce a sample not representative of the target population. Since pupils, parents and staff are selected from those available at Sports Day, their views may differ from those who are not present, introducing bias into the data gathered. 
    \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

[]{#re3a}

#### [Chapter 3 Review Exercise](#re3q) {-}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item Convenience sampling.
            \item This is a non-random sampling method which may produce a sample that is not representative of the target population, and may introduce bias to the data.
        \end{enumerate}
        \item
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item Simple random sampling.
            \item With the 150 employees in an ordered list, selecting 30 employees requires every fifth employee ($\frac{\text{150}}{\text{30}}$) to be selected. A random cell selection tool could be used to select the first employee to be included in the sample at random from the first 5. From there, every 5th employee on the list could be selected until the sample of size 30 has been obtained.
        \end{enumerate}
        \item
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item A numbered list of the restaurants in the chain could be obtained. A random number generator could be used to pick several numbers, and those restaurants corresponding to the numbers could be selected to be sampled. For a one-stage cluster sample, all employees at those restaurants should be sampled.
            \item One advantage of this method is that it will require less restaurants to be visited for an equivalent sample size, reducing travel costs. One disadvantage is that visiting employees at the same restaurant may have similar experiences. Selecting only a few restaurants may therefore give less precise results and may miss important differences among restaurants.
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}
    \item For an overall sample size of 150 out of 5000 (3\%), the sample needs to include 3 people from Management, 12 from Sales and 135 from the Shop Floor. For each stratum, an ordered sampling frame should be obtained, and numbers assigned. For the Management sample, a random number generator should be used to choose 3 numbers, and those staff corresponding to those numbers should be selected to be in the sample. The same process should be repeated to choose 12 from the Sales sampling frame, and 135 from the Shop Floor sampling frame. Put together, this will make a sample of size 150 with proportions from each stratum matching those of the target population.
    \item The pizzas sampled will only be those from takeaway restaurants, and may not be representative of pizzas sold in the UK as a whole. Additionally, only those takeaways in the nutritionist's local area will be included, rather than the UK as a whole. (Or, only those takeaways with a presence on social media will be included).
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item It is unlikely to be possible for the researcher to obtain a list of all pupils in Scotland studying Higher Mathematics.
        \item Obtain a sampling frame of centres presenting pupils for Higher Mathematics and randomly select a number of centres using simple random sampling. For each selected centre, obtain a list of its Higher Mathematics pupils and use simple random sampling to select a specified number of pupils. Combine the selected pupils to form the sample.
    \end{enumerate}
    \item A random letter selector and a random number generator could be used together to select a letter and a number, to correspond to the grid references, such as 'C' and '5' to select grid C5. This process could be repeated to create a list of boxes for the botanist to visit and study the health of flowers in those boxes.
\end{enumerate}

#### [Exercise 5.2](#ex52q) {-}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item $r=\text{0.971}$ suggests a strong positive linear correlation between red squirrel tail length and height.
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $r=\text{0.565}$ suggests a moderate positive linear correlation between age and finishing time.
        \item $r=-\text{0.980}$ suggests a very strong negative linear correlation between age and selling price.
    \end{enumerate}
    \item $r=\text{0.857}$ suggests a strong positive linear correlation between homework marks and test scores.
    \item
    \begin{enumerate} 
        \item The word "proves" is inappropriate because $r=-\text{0.206}$ comes from a sample, not a full population.
        \item The data appears to be made up of two distinct groups. The researcher should consider each group separately, calculating a sample correlation coefficient for each.
        \item The scatterplot should show labels for each axis, and scales for each axis. (Also the different types of iris could be represented with different colours or symbols).
    \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

#### [Exercise 5.3](#ex53q) {-}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\hat{y}=94.867-0.846x$
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\hat{y}=40.551+4.735x$
        \item approximately 59.0 feet
    \end{enumerate}
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\hat{y}=194.817-23.483x$
        \item $r=-0.928$, suggesting a very strong negative linear relationship between finishing times and training miles.
        \item The equation is unsuitable because it is a regression line of distance on time ($y$ on $x$). The website wishes to predict time from distance, which requires a regression line of time on distance ($x$ on $y$).
    \end{enumerate}
    \pagebreak
    \item 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\hat{y}=63.119-0.521x$
        \item $\hat{y}=60.5$ minutes
    \end{enumerate}

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The scatterplot suggests a strong positive linear relationship between back squat weight and vertical jump height.
        \item $r=0.829$, suggesting a strong positive linear correlation between back squat weight and vertical jump height.
        \item 
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item $\hat{y}=7.237+0.3593x$
            \item $\hat{y}=66.5$cm. This estimate may be considered reasonably reliable since it is interpolation and the correlation is strong.
        \end{enumerate}
        \item This advice may not be correct since correlation does not imply causation; a correlation between squat weight and jump height does not necessarily mean increasing squat weight will lead to an increase in jump height. There may be other factors influencing both variables.
    \end{enumerate}
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\hat{y}=36.63-0.0392x$
        \item They may have observed that the scatterplot did not seem to show any linear relationship between the variables, and so obtaining the equation of a least squares regression line would not have been appropriate.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}

#### [Exercise 7.6](#ex76q) {-}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Arrivals may occur in groups, so people may not arrive singly. The arrival rate may also vary throughout the day.
        \item The amount of rain is a continuous measurement, whereas a Poisson random variable counts discrete events.
        \item Vehicles may arrive in groups because their movements are affected by traffic flow and nearby traffic lights. The events may therefore not be independent, and the mean rate may not be constant.
        \item Buses normally follow a timetable, so their arrivals are not random throughout the interval.
        \item The checks may not be independent, and the mean rate may vary during the match, for example at half-time or following an important incident.
    \end{enumerate}

        \item Since 420 centimetres lies within the confidence interval, there is insufficient evidence to suggest that the population mean length of the bars has changed from 420 centimetres.

    \item $(\pounds\text{10.11},\pounds\text{11.69})$.\newline
    Since £12 lies outwith the confidence interval, there is sufficient evidence to suggest that the population mean annual amount spent on photocopying per teacher differs from £12. The previously used figure of £12 may therefore no longer be accurate.

    \item Assuming that the sample standard deviation of 0.6 goals is a reasonable estimate of the population standard deviation, the 99\% confidence interval is $(\text{2.438},\text{2.962})$ goals.\newline
    Since 2.5 goals lies within the confidence interval, there is insufficient evidence to suggest that the population mean number of goals scored per game has changed from 2.5.

    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Assume that the population standard deviation of mature oak-tree heights remains unchanged at 1.5 metres.\newline
        $(\text{19.95},\text{20.85})$ metres.

        \item Since 21 metres lies outwith the confidence interval, there is sufficient evidence to suggest that the population mean height of mature oak trees in the woodland has changed from 21 metres.
    \end{enumerate}

    \item
    \begin{enumerate}
